hero.heading: Hardware that works well with Crustates.
hero.lead: Crustates runs on most 64-bit machines from the last ten years, on amd64 and arm64. This guide covers what to buy, what to avoid and how the installer checks your box.

specs.heading: Minimum and recommended.
rows: 6–8 cores with VT-d / AMD-Vi (IOMMU); Intel Quick Sync for media
32 GB; ECC if the board supports it
Optional (small pool on the boot disk)
2.5 GbE or faster; a second port for VLANs
UEFI with Secure Boot and TPM 2.0
Ryzen 5/7 or 12th-gen+ Core i5, 32 GB, two disks

paragraphs.text: Intel VT-x or AMD-V is required; VT-d or AMD-Vi (IOMMU) for passthrough.
a GICv3 interrupt controller with ITS is needed for Cloud Hypervisor microVMs. Boards without it run apps as QEMU microvm or shared containers.
Platform: about 1 GB. Each app microVM: tens of MB overhead plus the app. Windows VM: 4–8 GB. ZFS ARC: likes spare RAM and gives it back. Local LLM: 8–16 GB for a 7–14B model.
is recommended for storage boxes, not required.
The OS is a read-only image on its own small SSD. Data lives on separate pool disks, so you can reinstall or replace the boot disk without touching your data.
ZFS and Btrfs want to see every disk directly. Use onboard SATA or an HBA flashed to IT mode. Hardware RAID controllers hide disk health and break self-healing.
Intel and Mellanox NICs are the safe choice. Realtek 2.5 GbE works with the in-kernel driver. A second port lets you split management and VM traffic.
Intel iGPUs can be shared with apps for Jellyfin or Plex transcoding. A dedicated NVIDIA or AMD card can be passed to one VM or used for a local model behind the AI assistant.

pi.title: Raspberry Pi 5.
pi.body: The Pi 5 has no GICv3-ITS, so Cloud Hypervisor microVMs are not available; apps fall back to QEMU microvm or isolation: shared. Booting the image on the Pi is still being verified.

installer.heading: The installer checks your box first.
installer.lead: Before it writes anything, the installer tests virtualisation, IOMMU groups, Secure Boot and TPM, disk health and NIC drivers, and tells you what will and won't work.

support.heading: Fedora’s kernel, plus the drivers we sign.
support.lead: Crustates runs Fedora’s kernel, pinned per release, so support is mainline Linux plus linux-firmware. Anything outside the kernel (ZFS, NVIDIA, Coral, Hailo) is built and signed in our CI and boot-tested before a release ships.

nics.lead: Bonds and VLANs are set up in Current, on top of any supported adapter.

arm.lead: arm64 is a first-class target; how much works depends on upstream kernel support for each board.

secureBoot.heading: Signed drivers, one key.
secureBoot.body: ZFS, NVIDIA, Coral and Hailo drivers live outside Fedora’s kernel, so Crustates signs them with its own key. On a Secure Boot machine you enrol that key once (MOK) during install; after that every update just boots.
points: The public key and its fingerprint are published
Every image is boot-tested in CI with the drivers loaded
Never turn Secure Boot off to make a driver load

hcl.heading: Tested on real boxes.
hcl.body: The installer’s hardware check can send an anonymous report (opt-in): CPU, board, NICs, GPUs, controllers and what worked. Those reports fill a searchable compatibility list.
